docs.title: Atlas guide
docs.text:
Atlas is a game metadata server. It gathers what many providers (Steam, IGDB, RAWG…) and a community say about a game, merges it into one canonical record, and keeps track of where every detail came from. Other programs, above all the Unnamed Tracking App, read that record through an API. People browse and improve it on Atlas's own website.

It is designed to be run by many people:

  • a central authority that a community curates,
  • mirrors that copy it for speed and resilience,
  • local nodes that cache providers for one household and can still follow a central node.

Everything an operator normally wants to change (name, colours, logo, menus, pages, extra fields, limits, email, who may sign in how) is a setting in the admin UI. You should not need to change code to run your own Atlas.

docs.title: Where to start
docs.text: I want to… Read try it in five minutes Quick start understand how records are built Concepts use or contribute to a site Using the site review other people's changes Reviewing run and configure a node Administering, Deployment run several nodes Federation, Sign-in sharing connect the Tracking App Tracking App call the API API reference look up a setting Environment variables, Admin settings understand the safety model Security add providers or fields Extending fix a problem Troubleshooting

docs.title: What it is not
docs.text:
• Not a tracker. Atlas holds facts about games. Playtime, ownership and completion belong to the app that tracks them. Atlas deliberately discards personal facts it is sent.
  • Not a store of provider data to redistribute. Provider-derived data stays on the node that fetched it. Only what people contribute (released as CC0) is replicated.

Contributed metadata is dedicated to the public domain under CC0 1.0; the software is MIT.

docs.title: Administering a node
docs.text: Everything here is in the Admin area (administrators only). Almost nothing needs a restart or a code change.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Admin → Overview shows the node's role and id, replication position, providers, users (role, status, email state, external sign-in permission) and a recent activity log: settings changed, proposals decided, roles changed, tokens created, peers added. Every moderation and admin action is recorded with who did it.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Changes apply within seconds on every process, are validated, are recorded in the log, and can be undone with Use default. The full list with defaults is in Admin settings. Groups:

  • Branding: site name, tagline, footer, accent colours (dark/light), theme (auto/dark/light), navigation links, logo.
  • Community: registration open/closed, email policy, reputation thresholds, proposal limits, comments and lists on/off with limits.
  • Security: password length, sign-in lifetime, API rate limit, batch sizes.
  • Matching: automatic-merge and review confidence.
  • Artwork: caching on/off and size limit.
  • Email: delivery mode, SMTP host/port/user/STARTTLS, from address.
  • Federation: adopt upstream media types/fields; act as a sign-in provider.

Things deliberately not editable here (environment only): database URL, role, public URL, secret key, SMTP password, bootstrap token. See Environment variables.

docs.title: Logo and navigation
docs.text: Upload a PNG/JPEG/WebP/GIF (≤512 KB, ≤1024 px; checked and re-served from the node). Navigation links are Label | address lines; addresses are /paths or https:// only.

docs.title: Pages
docs.text: Admin → Pages writes About, Rules, Help or anything else in Markdown (headings, lists, emphasis, links; raw HTML and images are ignored for safety). Pages can be drafts, ordered, and shown in the top menu. Three starter pages exist.

docs.title: Media types and custom fields
docs.text:
Admin → Fields. A media type says what a record is (game is built in; add movie, anime, tool…). For each type you can:

  • rename core fields, so a movie's Developer reads Director and Publisher reads Studio;
  • add custom fields: text, long text, number, date, yes/no, choice (with options), list, link (https://). Each has a label, help text, order, shown (page and API) and editable by contributors switches.

Custom values appear on the page, in the contributor form and the API (custom), are merged by source trust like core fields, can be proposed, reviewed and reverted, and move with records when merged. A field's kind cannot change after creation (create a new field instead). Deleting a field deletes its values. A type that has records can only be disabled, not deleted.

Authorities replicate their types and fields to mirrors and local nodes (Settings → Adopt the upstream media types and fields); a node's own definitions always win over an upstream one of the same name.

docs.title: Email
docs.text:
Set Email → Delivery to smtp and fill host, port, user and from; put the password in ATLAS_SMTP_PASSWORD. Messages are queued and sent by a background worker with retries and backoff, so a slow mail server never slows a page. Admin → Email lists every message and its state. With delivery outbox (the default) nothing is sent; the admin can read the messages, which is enough to try sign-up and password reset or to run a private node.

Email verification policy: required (default on authorities) means people confirm an address before they can contribute or comment; optional (default on other nodes) asks but doesn't block; off doesn't ask. Administrators are never blocked. Mark confirmed in the user list helps when mail isn't configured.

docs.title: Users
docs.text: Admin → Overview → Users: set a role (user, curator, admin) and status (active, suspended). Suspending signs the person out everywhere and revokes their tokens. You cannot demote or suspend yourself. The first administrator is ATLAS_INITIAL_ADMIN (or the first account); atlas make-admin <username> promotes someone from the command line.

docs.title: Tokens
docs.text: Admin → Tokens creates service tokens (for apps, mirrors, scripts) with scopes and optional expiry, shows the secret once, lists last use, and revokes. Scopes: read, contribute, curate, sync (replication), admin. People's own personal tokens appear here too (read-only, with their owner).

docs.title: Peers and sign-in sharing
docs.text:
• Admin → Peers: nodes this one replicates from. See Federation.
  • Admin → Sign-in sharing: OpenID Connect both ways. See Sign-in sharing.

docs.title: Moderation
docs.text: Reviewers handle proposals, duplicates and reported comments (Reviewing). Administrators can also change anyone's role.

docs.title: Routine care
docs.text:
• Back up the database and the media volume (Deployment).
  • After upgrades, check Admin → Overview shows the feed head and no peer errors.
  • Review the activity log occasionally; it is your audit trail.

docs.title: Observations and canonical records
docs.text:
Atlas never edits a record directly. Everything it learns is an observation: one source's claim about one thing ("Steam says app 620 is Portal 2, released 2011-04-19, by Valve"). Observations are kept, not overwritten; a newer one from the same source supersedes the older for merging, and the old one stays as history.

A canonical record (atlas:01m5…) is derived from the current observations of everything that was matched to it. Because it is derived, it can always be rebuilt, explained, split or merged again.

docs.title: How fields are merged
docs.text:
Each field has a rule, and Atlas records which observation won (see Where this came from on every game page and GET /games/{id}/explain):

Field Rule title, description, developer, publisher, series highest trust wins; ties go to the newest release date trust-weighted vote across sources platforms, genres/tags, features union (case-insensitive, up to 100) identifiers each source's own id plus the ids it cross-references; the most trusted claim wins a namespace custom fields the most trusted source's value anything a curator can pin a value; a pin beats everything

Trust is a number per source (curator 100, manual 90, community 85, igdb 70, steam 65, gog 60, rawg 50, others 40). Names that carry weight are reserved: only a token with the curate scope (or the node itself) may submit under them, so nobody can impersonate a trusted source.

docs.title: Matching: which record does a claim belong to?
docs.text:
1. Identifiers. If the source's own id, or an id it cross-references, is already known, that settles it.
  2. Title evidence. Same normalised title (accents, ™, editions and numerals ignored; Mega Man X ≠ Mega Man 10) and same release year scores high enough to merge automatically. A missing year, a different year, or only a fuzzy title does not.
  3. Anything uncertain creates a separate record and opens a possible duplicate for a person to decide. Atlas prefers a duplicate someone can merge over a wrong merge nobody notices.

Merging leaves a redirect, so ids held by other programs keep working. A wrong merge can be split (detach a source record).

docs.title: What is not stored
docs.text: Playtime, ownership, wishlist state, favourites and similar personal facts are stripped from submissions on arrival. Accounts, lists and follows exist on the website for people who choose to use them, and can be exported or deleted (see Using the site).

docs.title: Media types and custom fields
docs.text: A record has a media type (game is built in). An admin can add types (movie, anime…) and extra typed fields per type, and can relabel core fields per type (a movie's Developer reads Director). They appear in forms, pages and the API, and contributors' changes to them are reviewed like any other. See Administering.

docs.title: Artwork and achievements
docs.text:
• Artwork is stored as references (kind, address, size). The server downloads an image only after safety checks and then serves its own copy by content hash; pages never hotlink a provider.
  • Achievements are the list for a game: name, description, icon, hidden flag, global unlock percentage. Never anyone's progress.

docs.title: Nodes and roles
docs.text:
One program, three roles. See Federation.

Role Typical use Database authority the public source of truth; publishes a signed change feed PostgreSQL mirror a regional or read-heavy copy of an authority PostgreSQL or SQLite local one household or team; caches providers; may follow an authority SQLite

docs.title: Accounts and reputation
docs.text: Accounts belong to a node. Contributors propose changes; reviewers approve them. Approved work earns reputation; reputation unlocks faster paths. Details in Using the site and Reviewing.

docs.title: Choose a shape
docs.text:
Local node Public authority Compose file compose.yaml compose.authority.yaml Database SQLite in a volume PostgreSQL 16 Role local authority TLS usually none (localhost/LAN) required, via a reverse proxy Email outbox is fine real SMTP recommended (verification and reset are on by default)

Verified: the container image builds, runs as a non-root user, keeps data across restarts and reports healthy; the authority stack (Atlas + PostgreSQL + a one-shot migration job) starts in production mode.

docs.title: Production checklist (authority)
docs.text:
1. A host with Docker Compose and a DNS name, e.g. atlas.example.org.
  2. .env (see .env.example): 
    ATLAS_ROLE=authority
ATLAS_ENVIRONMENT=production
ATLAS_PUBLIC_URL=https://atlas.example.org
ATLAS_INITIAL_ADMIN=alice
ATLAS_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_TOKEN=<32+ random characters>
ATLAS_SECRET_KEY=<atlas secret-key>
POSTGRES_PASSWORD=<strong>
ATLAS_MAIL_BACKEND=smtp
ATLAS_SMTP_HOST=smtp.example.org
ATLAS_SMTP_USER=…
ATLAS_SMTP_PASSWORD=…
ATLAS_MAIL_FROM=Atlas <noreply@example.org>
    Production mode refuses to start unless: HTTPS public URL, PostgreSQL for an authority, and (with open registration) an initial admin or bootstrap token.
  3. docker compose -f compose.authority.yaml up -d. It runs atlas migrate first, then the server (bound to 127.0.0.1:8000; never publish PostgreSQL).
  4. Put a TLS-terminating reverse proxy in front.

docs.title: Reverse proxy
docs.text:
The app must see the visitor's address for rate limits, so the proxy must send X-Forwarded-For/X-Forwarded-Proto, and the server must trust only the proxy (the authority compose file uses --forwarded-allow-ips "*", which is safe only because the port is bound to localhost behind your proxy).

Caddy: 

atlas.example.org {
    encode zstd gzip
    reverse_proxy 127.0.0.1:8000
}
nginx: 
server {
    server_name atlas.example.org;
    client_max_body_size 4m;
    location / {
        proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:8000;
        proxy_set_header Host $host;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $remote_addr;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;
    }
}
(plus your usual TLS configuration).

docs.title: Backups
docs.text:
What to back up:

  1. The database (pg_dump -Fc for PostgreSQL; the volume or sqlite3 .backup for SQLite). It contains the records, accounts, settings and the node's signing keys (identity), so followers keep trusting a restored node.
  2. The media volume (ATLAS_MEDIA_DIR). It can be re-downloaded (provider artwork) but community-uploaded logos cannot.
  3. Your .env, especially ATLAS_SECRET_KEY: without it stored peer tokens and OIDC client secrets cannot be decrypted (you would re-enter them).

Restore: new host, same .env, restore the database and media, docker compose up -d. Test a restore before you need it.

docs.title: Upgrading
docs.text:
1. Back up (above).
  2. git pull, then docker compose -f compose.authority.yaml up -d --build (the migration job runs first). With several replicas set ATLAS_AUTO_MIGRATE=false and run atlas migrate once as a job.
  3. Migrations are forward-only; to roll back, restore the backup.

docs.title: Operating
docs.text:
• Health: GET /api/v2/health (liveness), /api/v2/ready (database), /api/v2/status (admin: feed head, replication).
  • Logs: plain uvicorn logs on stdout. Structured logs and metrics are not built yet.
  • Scaling: more replicas are fine (rate limits, sessions and tokens live in the database); one writer holds a lock at a time. No load figures have been measured; plan capacity by testing your own workload.
  • Housekeeping: background threads in each process send email, cache artwork, purge expired counters/tokens and pull from peers. atlas cache-media runs a caching pass by hand.

docs.title: Command line
docs.text:
atlas serve | migrate | token | node | secret-key | sync | cache-media | make-admin | import-legacy (docker compose exec atlas atlas <command>). import-legacy <demo-1.db> migrates data from the earlier demo version (release dates were year-only there and are dropped).

For every environment variable: Environment variables.

docs.title: Extending Atlas
docs.text: Most customisation needs no code (Administering). For the rest:

docs.title: A client of the API
docs.text: Any language can call the REST API. A single-file Python client lives in clients/python/atlas_client.py (search, game, resolve, provider_search/fetch, submit). The ingestion format is the Tracking App's observation contract v1 (atlas/contract.py); Atlas adds only optional fields (platforms) and never removes any, so clients written against the contract keep working.

docs.title: A new metadata provider
docs.text:
A provider is a small class in atlas/providers/:

class MyProvider:
    name = "mysource"            # becomes the source name and namespace
    redistributable = False       # provider data is never published on the feed
    requests_per_minute = 60      # shared budget; searches get a third of it

    def search(self, client, query) -> list[ProviderResult]: ...
    def fetch(self, client, external_id) -> ProviderResult | None: ...
    def achievements(self, client, external_id) -> list[dict]: ...   # optional

ProviderResult carries external_id, title, optional release_date (ISO), platform, provider_ids (cross-references to other providers: these are what merge records), facts (description, developer, publisher, tags, features), artwork and achievements. Register it in build_registry (atlas/providers/registry.py) behind a setting. The Fetcher adds caching, negative caching, per-provider budgets, a circuit breaker and serve-stale-on-error for you. Give the source a trust weight in source_trust and add tests with recorded response shapes (see tests/test_providers.py).

docs.title: A new field type or merge rule
docs.text: Merge rules are in atlas/merge.py (one function, rules per field). Custom field kinds are in atlas/custom.py (validate_value plus the form input in _fields.html). Keep every rule deterministic and explainable: record which observation won.

docs.title: Keeping docs honest
docs.text: python tools/gen_docs.py regenerates the three reference pages from the code; the test suite fails if they are stale or if a setting or endpoint is undocumented.

docs.title: Federation
docs.text: Atlas nodes can follow each other. There is no central server in the code: any node can be an authority for its own community, and others can follow it.

docs.title: Roles
docs.text: Role Writes Replicates from Notes authority accepts contributions and curation; publishes the signed change feed nobody PostgreSQL in production mirror provider cache and local-only overlays an authority can't rewrite records the upstream owns local everything on its own data optionally an authority SQLite; private overlays win locally

docs.title: What replicates
docs.text:
Only things that are safe to republish:

  • curated and community observations (sources curator, manual, community by default),
  • merges, splits and pinned fields made on the authority,
  • curated artwork and achievements, and curated custom-field values,
  • media types and custom-field definitions (if the receiver adopts them).

What does not replicate: provider data (Steam, IGDB…; each node fetches its own under the provider's terms), accounts, passwords, reputation, comments, lists, follows, notifications, settings and pages. Mirrors and local nodes keep everything they cache themselves.

docs.title: How trust works
docs.text:
• Every node has an Ed25519 identity (its node id is a short fingerprint of the key). Look at Admin → Peers → This node.
  • Each feed entry is signed (covering its sequence number, kind and content). A receiver accepts entries only from keys the administrator pinned.
  • Entries must arrive in order with no gaps. A gap, a rewind, a bad signature, a different key or an altered kind is refused and nothing from that batch is applied.
  • If the upstream is unreachable, the node keeps serving what it has and retries with backoff.

docs.title: Setting up a mirror or local node that follows an authority
docs.text:
On the authority (administrator):

  1. Admin → Tokens: create a token with scopes read and sync for the follower.
  2. Tell the follower's administrator the authority's address and its node id (Admin → Peers → This node) by a channel you trust (not only the same web page).

On the follower (set ATLAS_ROLE=mirror or local, and ATLAS_SECRET_KEY so the token can be stored encrypted):

  1. Admin → Peers → Add a peer: address + token → Look up node.
  2. Atlas shows the node's id. Compare it with what you were told. Then Trust this node and replicate from it.
  3. Sync now to pull immediately; afterwards it follows every ATLAS_SYNC_INTERVAL_SECONDS (60 by default). The peer list shows position, last success and any error.

You can also configure a single upstream with environment variables (ATLAS_UPSTREAM_URL, ATLAS_UPSTREAM_TOKEN, ATLAS_TRUSTED_KEYS; see Environment variables); use whichever you prefer, and you can follow several peers from the UI.

docs.title: Local changes on a follower
docs.text:
• A follower cannot merge, split or unpin records the upstream owns (those decisions belong to the authority). Pins a follower sets are local-only, never override upstream ones, and an upstream pin never overwrites a local override. Edits proposed on a follower are local overlays and are never sent upstream.
  • A record the follower created from a provider folds into the authoritative record when an upstream observation claims the same identifiers (authority wins; no duplicates).
  • Local nodes can add their own media types and fields; those stay local and win over an upstream definition with the same name.

docs.title: Operating it
docs.text:
• Position/lag: Admin → Peers shows each peer's position; GET /api/v2/status (admin) shows the authority's feed head.
  • Add a mirror: nothing to do on the authority except issue a token.
  • Remove a peer: Remove; data already received stays.
  • Disaster recovery: a node's identity (signing key) lives in its database; restoring the database restores the identity and followers keep working. Promoting a mirror to authority is not supported yet, because a mirror has a different identity; plan recovery around database backups (Deployment).
  • Several workers: every worker process runs the sync loop; replays are idempotent, so extra pulls are wasteful but harmless.
  • One writer at a time: writes are serialised by a database lock. This is fine for metadata; it is the first thing to revisit under very heavy ingestion.

docs.title: Sharing sign-ins between nodes
docs.text: Separate from replication: Sign-in sharing.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text: You need Docker with the Compose plugin. Five minutes, no accounts elsewhere.

docs.title: 1. Start a node
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/obsoletelabs/unnamed_tracking_metadata.git
cd unnamed_tracking_metadata && git checkout v2
cp .env.example .env

Edit .env:

ATLAS_ROLE=local
ATLAS_PUBLIC_URL=http://localhost:8000
ATLAS_INITIAL_ADMIN=alice            # the username that will administer this node
ATLAS_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_TOKEN=         # 32+ random characters, e.g. `openssl rand -hex 24`

docker compose up -d

Open http://localhost:8000. A local node keeps its data in a Docker volume (SQLite) and sends no email (messages are listed under Admin → Email instead).

docs.title: 2. Become the administrator
docs.text: Choose Create account and register with the username you put in ATLAS_INITIAL_ADMIN. That account is the administrator. (If you leave the setting empty, the first account to register is.)

docs.title: 3. Add some games
docs.text:
• From the site: Add game (your proposal; the administrator's applies at once).
  • From a provider: POST /api/v2/providers/steam/fetch {"external_id": "620"} with a token, which downloads, merges and stores the record.
TOKEN=$ATLAS_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_TOKEN
curl -s localhost:8000/api/v2/providers/steam/fetch -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
     -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{"external_id":"620"}'

docs.title: 4. Create a token for other programs
docs.text:
Admin → Tokens → name it, tick read → copy the secret (shown once). Or from the command line: docker compose exec atlas atlas token --name tracker --scopes read.

curl -s 'localhost:8000/api/v2/games?q=portal' -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>"

docs.title: 5. Make it yours
docs.text: Admin → Settings changes the name, colours, logo, menu links, registration, email and limits live. Admin → Pages edits About/Rules/Help. Admin → Fields adds extra fields (for example Engine or Age rating). See Administering.

docs.title: Next
docs.text:
• A shared, public node? Read Deployment (PostgreSQL, HTTPS, email) and set ATLAS_ROLE=authority.
  • Follow a central node from home? Federation.
  • Use it from the Tracking App: Tracking App.

Command-line tools (atlas <command>): serve, migrate, token, node, secret-key, sync, cache-media, make-admin, import-legacy.

docs.title: API reference
docs.text:
Generated by tools/gen_docs.py from the code. Do not edit by hand.

Base path /api/v2. Send Authorization: Bearer <token>. Scopes: read, contribute, curate, sync, admin (admin implies all). Endpoints marked public need no token. Errors are {"error": {"code", "message"}}; validation errors are 422; limits return 429 with Retry-After.

docs.title: ops
docs.text: Method Path Scope What it does GET /health public Liveness: the process is up. GET /ready public Readiness: the database answers. GET /schema public Media types and custom fields this node describes (public ones only). GET /site public Name, theme, navigation, role, registration and email policy of this node.

docs.title: read
docs.text: Method Path Scope What it does GET /games read Search records by title (q, optional type, limit). Includes custom values. GET /games/{cid} read One record. Follows merge redirects (redirected_from). ETag = id-version. GET /games/{cid}/achievements read Merged achievement list: name, description, icon, hidden, global percent. No per-user progress. GET /games/{cid}/artwork read Artwork by trust and priority, plus the best image per kind; media_url once cached. GET /games/{cid}/explain read Which source and rule produced each field (provenance). GET /media/{digest} read A cached, verified image. Immutable; nosniff. POST /resolve read Batch (max max_resolve): store ids / titles to canonical ids with method and confidence. Read-only.

docs.title: write
docs.text: Method Path Scope What it does POST /observations contribute Submit a batch of observations (the app's ingestion contract v1). Personal facts are discarded.

docs.title: curate
docs.text: Method Path Scope What it does PUT /games/{cid}/achievements curate Replace the curated achievement set for a record. PUT /games/{cid}/artwork curate Replace the curated artwork set for a record. PUT /games/{cid}/custom curate Set or clear curated custom-field values. DELETE /games/{cid}/locks/{field} curate Remove a pinned field value. PUT /games/{cid}/locks/{field} curate Pin a field value; it beats every merged value. POST /games/{cid}/merge curate Merge a record into another (leaves a redirect). GET /games/{cid}/observations curate Raw source records behind a record (current and superseded). POST /observations/{oid}/detach curate Split one source record off onto its own record. GET /review curate Open possible-duplicate and id-conflict items. POST /review/{rid}/dismiss curate Mark a review item as not a duplicate. POST /review/{rid}/merge curate Resolve a review item by merging into one of its candidates.

docs.title: providers
docs.text: Method Path Scope What it does GET /providers read Providers configured on this node and their request budgets. POST /providers/{name}/fetch contribute Fetch full details from a provider (cached), merge, return the record. GET /providers/{name}/search read Lightweight provider search; nothing is stored.

docs.title: federation
docs.text: Method Path Scope What it does GET /sync/changes sync The signed change feed after since (replication). GET /sync/info read This node's id, public key and role (what a peer pins).

docs.title: admin
docs.text: Method Path Scope What it does GET /status admin Role, feed head and replication cursors. GET /tokens admin List API tokens. POST /tokens admin Create a token; the secret is returned once. DELETE /tokens/{tid} admin Revoke a token.

docs.title: Environment variables
docs.text:
Generated by tools/gen_docs.py from the code. Do not edit by hand.

Every setting is read from an environment variable named ATLAS_<NAME> (or from a .env file). Settings marked live can also be changed at runtime in Admin → Settings; the environment value is then only the default.

docs.title: Node
docs.text: Variable Default Meaning ATLAS_ROLE local authority (the source of truth; publishes the signed change feed), mirror (replicates an authority) or local (a private node that caches providers and may replicate). ATLAS_DATABASE_URL sqlite:///./atlas.db SQLAlchemy URL. sqlite:///./atlas.db for local nodes; postgresql+psycopg://user:pw@host/db for authorities (required in production). ATLAS_PUBLIC_URL http://localhost:8000 The address people use to reach this node. Used in emails, OIDC and links. Must be https:// in production. ATLAS_ENVIRONMENT dev dev shows API docs at /docs and relaxes production checks; production enforces HTTPS, PostgreSQL for authorities and an explicit initial administrator. ATLAS_INITIAL_ADMIN — Username that becomes the website administrator when it registers. If unset, the first account to register is the administrator (production with open registration refuses to start without it). ATLAS_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_TOKEN — 32+ random characters. Becomes an admin API token while set; removing it revokes it. Use it to create the first real tokens. ATLAS_SECRET_KEY — Encrypts secrets stored in the database (peer tokens, OIDC client secrets). Generate one with atlas secret-key. Losing it makes those secrets unreadable. ATLAS_AUTO_MIGRATE — Run database migrations on start. Default: on for SQLite, off otherwise. With several replicas set false and run atlas migrate as a job.

docs.title: Federation
docs.text: Variable Default Meaning ATLAS_UPSTREAM_URL — Address of an upstream node to replicate from (simple single-upstream setups; more can be added under Admin → Peers). ATLAS_UPSTREAM_TOKEN — API token (scopes read, sync) for upstream_url. ATLAS_TRUSTED_KEYS — JSON object {"<node id>": "<base64 public key>"} of upstream nodes whose signed feed you trust. Required when upstream_url is set. Get the values from atlas node on the upstream. ATLAS_SYNC_INTERVAL_SECONDS 60 How often to pull from peers (minimum 5). ATLAS_SYNC_BATCH_SIZE 500 Feed entries fetched per request. ATLAS_INHERIT_SCHEMA true Adopt the upstream authority's media types and custom fields (yours always take precedence). Editable in Admin → Settings. live ATLAS_OIDC_PROVIDER_ENABLED false Let other nodes and the Tracking App sign users in with accounts on this node (OpenID Connect). Editable in Admin → Settings. live

docs.title: Matching
docs.text: Variable Default Meaning ATLAS_AUTO_MATCH_THRESHOLD 0.85 Confidence (0.5–1.0) at or above which an incoming record is merged into an existing one automatically. Editable as a percentage in Admin → Settings. live ATLAS_REVIEW_THRESHOLD 0.6 Confidence below the auto threshold but above this opens a possible-duplicate review. live ATLAS_SOURCE_TRUST {'curator': 100, 'manual': 90, 'community': 85, 'igdb': 70, 'steam': 65, 'gog': 60, 'rawg': 50} JSON object of source name → trust weight used to choose between conflicting values (higher wins). Reserved names need the curate scope to submit. ATLAS_DEFAULT_TRUST 40 Trust for sources not listed in source_trust (apps and plugins submitting data). ATLAS_REDISTRIBUTABLE_SOURCES ['community', 'curator', 'manual'] Sources whose curated observations are published on the change feed. Provider data (Steam, IGDB…) is never federated.

docs.title: Limits
