docs.title: Reviewing
docs.text: You can review if an administrator made you a curator, or your reputation reached the node's threshold (500 by default). You cannot review your own proposals (administrators may).

docs.title: The queue
docs.text:
Review lists pending proposals oldest first, each as a diff. Approve applies the change and rewards the contributor; Reject explains why (the note is shown to them). Open a proposal's Discuss link to ask a question first.

Good review habits: check the cited source; approve improvements even if imperfect; reject unsupported or promotional changes; leave a short note either way.

docs.title: Possible duplicates
docs.text: Review → Possible duplicates lists records Atlas was not sure about (possible_duplicate) or whose identifiers disagree (id_conflict), with a confidence. Merge into this folds the record into the other (a redirect remains); Not duplicates dismisses it.

docs.title: On a game page
docs.text:
Reviewers also see Curation:

  • Merge into another record by id.
  • Pinned fields: fix a value permanently (beats every source). Unpin later.
  • Source records: every observation behind the record; Split off moves a wrongly merged source record onto its own game.
  • Revert a change: undo an approved community change. Reverts go newest first, because each restores the state before that change.

docs.title: Comments
docs.text: Review → Reported comments shows reported and auto-hidden comments. Hide removes it from view (the author loses 3 reputation); Keep visible dismisses the reports.

docs.title: Things that cannot happen by accident
docs.text:
• Reviews, reverts and withdrawals are serialised, so two reviewers never apply or pay for the same proposal twice.
  • Everything you do is in the audit log (Admin → Overview).

docs.title: What is protected, and how
docs.text:
Area Controls Accounts scrypt password hashing; server-side sessions stored hashed; HttpOnly, SameSite=Lax (and Secure over HTTPS) cookies; per-address and per-account throttling on sign-in, registration, reset and verification; identical answers for known and unknown accounts Forms a CSRF token on every state-changing form; strict Content-Security-Policy with no inline script or style; clickjacking and sniffing headers; user text is always escaped; Markdown pages cannot contain HTML API tokens stored only as hashes, scoped, expiring, revocable, fail-closed; personal tokens are read-only and die with the account; rate limits; body size caps; bounded batches Trust model reserved source names need curate; uncurated claims can match but cannot register identifiers in someone else's namespace; far-future timestamps ignored; personal facts discarded on arrival Artwork downloads only from public addresses (pinned address, every redirect re-checked, tunnelled IPv6 refused, environment proxies ignored), size and pixel limits, full image decode, content-hash storage, served with nosniff and a restrictive CSP Federation Ed25519-signed feed (sequence, kind, content), pinned trust, gap/rewind/tamper rejection, provider data never republished; even from a trusted peer, observations, schema and values are validated like local input and a malformed entry is skipped instead of stalling replication OIDC the sign-in is bound to the browser that started it (login-CSRF safe), exact redirect match, consent, PKCE, single-use burned codes, pinned issuer keys, algorithm never negotiated, email never used to take over an account Secrets at rest peer tokens and client secrets encrypted with ATLAS_SECRET_KEY; SMTP password only in the environment; sent email bodies deleted from the outbox Concurrency writers serialised; reviews, reverts and withdrawals cannot double-apply; responses are sent only after commit Audit admin and moderation actions are logged with the actor

Two independent code reviews were carried out during development; every confirmed finding was fixed with a regression test (the test suite runs the attack paths, not just the happy paths), and the database-level races are exercised on real PostgreSQL.

docs.title: Known limits (be aware)
docs.text:
• No two-factor authentication yet.
  • No breached-password check; passwords are length-checked only.
  • Signing keys (the node's Ed25519 identity and the OIDC RSA key) are stored in the database; there is no in-app rotation yet.
  • Observability (structured logs, metrics, alerting) is minimal.
  • The SMTP server and the reverse proxy are yours to harden.
  • Admin-supplied URLs (peers, OIDC providers) are fetched by the server; only administrators can set them, and private addresses are allowed on purpose (LAN mirrors).
  • Change-email answers "already used" for taken addresses (rate-limited), so a signed-in user can test whether an address is registered.
  • Account deletion removes personal data but keeps accepted (CC0) contributions, detached from the person.

docs.title: Reporting a problem
docs.text: Open a private security advisory on the repository, or contact the repository owners directly. Please include steps to reproduce.

docs.title: Sign-in sharing (OpenID Connect)
docs.text:
Atlas can be an OpenID Connect provider: people who have an account on an Atlas node can use it to sign in to other software. Atlas can also accept sign-ins from another Atlas node. Accounts and reputation always stay per node.

Using this with the Unnamed Tracking App? Jump to Signing in to the Tracking App with Atlas.

docs.title: What Atlas offers
docs.text:
Flow Authorization Code (with a consent screen) Discovery https://<node>/.well-known/openid-configuration Endpoints /oidc/authorize, /oidc/token, /oidc/userinfo, /oidc/jwks Scopes openid (required), profile, email Client authentication client_secret_basic or client_secret_post PKCE S256; required by default, can be waived per confidential client ID token signature RS256 (default, works with almost everything) or EdDSA (for other Atlas nodes); both keys are in the JWKS Lifetimes authorization code 5 min (single use), ID token 10 min, access token 1 h Claims sub (stable account id), preferred_username, email, email_verified, atlas_reputation

Not offered: refresh tokens, dynamic client registration, RP-initiated or back-channel logout, group/role claims. Atlas never exports its roles: they are meaningful only on the node that granted them.

docs.title: 1. Turn the provider on
docs.text: Admin → Settings → Federation → Act as a sign-in provider (OIDC). Set ATLAS_PUBLIC_URL to the exact address people use (it is the issuer, and must be https:// in production). Check https://your-node/.well-known/openid-configuration answers.

docs.title: 2. Register the application
docs.text:
Admin → Sign-in sharing → Register application

  • Name: shown on the consent screen.
  • Redirect addresses: one per line, matched exactly. https://… or http://localhost… for testing. The application tells you its address (often https://app.example.org/…/callback).
  • Token signature: leave RS256 unless the application is another Atlas node.
  • Require PKCE: leave ticked if the application sends PKCE. Untick for confidential clients that cannot (the Tracking App's Authlib client is one).

You are shown a client id and client secret once. Atlas stores only a hash of the secret; if it is lost, delete the application and register it again.

docs.title: 3. Configure the application
docs.text:
Give it the issuer / discovery URL (https://your-node), the client id and secret, and scopes openid profile email. Almost every OIDC-capable application then needs nothing else, because it reads the discovery document.

If it asks for endpoints individually, use the ones in the table above. If it wants to map claims: username ← preferred_username, email ← email, unique id ← sub.

Match users by sub where you can. Usernames can change; sub cannot. Do not trust email_verified: false for account linking: Atlas sets it to true only for addresses the person has confirmed.

docs.title: Quick check with a few lines of Python
docs.text:
# pip install authlib httpx
from authlib.integrations.requests_client import OAuth2Session
import requests
disc = requests.get("https://your-node/.well-known/openid-configuration").json()
print(disc["issuer"], disc["id_token_signing_alg_values_supported"])

Atlas's repository contains a complete end-to-end check that drives the real Authlib client stack used by the Tracking App through a login against a live node: tools/compat/tracking_app_oidc.py.

People then see a consent screen the first time each sign-in happens:

docs.title: Accepting sign-ins from another Atlas node
docs.text:
On the node that should accept sign-ins (for example a household node signing in with the central one):

  1. On your node: Admin → Sign-in sharing → Accept sign-ins from another node → Look up provider. Atlas fetches its discovery and keys and shows the provider's node id fingerprint. Compare it with what the provider's administrator gave you. Atlas pins that key and will only accept ID tokens signed by it (the algorithm is never negotiated). The page also shows the exact redirect address to register.
  2. On the provider node, register an application as above with that redirect address and signature EdDSA; copy the client id and secret.
  3. Back on your node, enter the client id and secret (stored encrypted; needs ATLAS_SECRET_KEY) and choose:
  4. Every user here may link and use it (otherwise you enable it per user in the user list),
  5. Create an account on first sign-in,
  6. Trust the provider's confirmed email address.
  7. The sign-in page now shows a button for the provider.

How accounts are connected:

  • A person with an existing local account links it from Profile settings → Linked sign-ins (needs permission, above). Email addresses are never used to take over an existing account; if auto-create is on and the username is taken, a new account with a suffix is made.
  • Accounts created this way have no password. They can add one with Forgot password if they have an email, and cannot unlink their only way in.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Cause “unknown application or redirect address” The redirect in the request is not exactly one registered (check scheme, port, trailing slash). “PKCE with S256 is required” The client does not send PKCE; untick Require PKCE for that application. “issuer mismatch” / discovery fails in the app ATLAS_PUBLIC_URL differs from the address the app uses; they must match exactly. App says the email is missing The Atlas user has no email address; add one (and on central nodes confirm it). invalid_client Wrong secret, application disabled, or credentials sent in an unsupported way. invalid_grant Code reused, expired (5 min), redirect changed between steps, or PKCE verifier wrong. A reused code also revokes its tokens. Provider button missing on your node Provider disabled, or Accept sign-ins entry is switched off. “External sign-in is not enabled for this account” Allow the user (user list) or tick Every user… on the provider.

docs.title: Security notes
docs.text:
• Redirect addresses are exact-match, and an error for an unregistered address is shown on Atlas, never redirected to an unvetted site.
  • A person must consent each time. The consent screen names the application and what it receives.
  • Codes are single use and are burned by any attempt; replaying one revokes the tokens it produced.
  • ID tokens from other Atlas nodes are verified against the key you pinned, with issuer, audience, nonce, expiry and issued-at checks; alg: none and algorithm-confusion attempts are rejected (all tested).
  • Rotating the RSA signing key is not yet a one-click action.

docs.title: The Unnamed Tracking App
docs.text: Atlas works with the Unnamed Tracking App in two independent ways. Use either or both.

docs.title: Metadata: the Atlas provider plugin
docs.text: The plugin official.metadata-atlas (source in the plugins repository, pull request #64) adds Atlas as a metadata provider: search, merged metadata, artwork and a health check.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
1. Run an Atlas node (Quick start) and create a token with only the read scope (Admin → Tokens).
  2. Get the plugin package. The plugin repository's branch CI publishes an unsigned preview (unsigned-dist); or build one: python tools/build_packages.py produces official.metadata-atlas-<version>.utp. Signed releases come from the official publisher.
  3. In the app: Plugin Manager → install the .utp (unsigned previews need explicit consent) and grant the declared permissions.
  4. Open the provider's settings and enter Atlas server URL (https://atlas.example.org, optional path prefix) and Atlas API token (write-only, stored encrypted by the app).

docs.title: What it does
docs.text: Operation Behaviour Search GET /games?q=…; returns Atlas id plus the store ids Atlas has linked (steam, igdb…) Metadata by Atlas id, or for a candidate that only has other providers' ids, by those ids or exact title+year. Only a certain match is accepted; uncertain returns nothing Media artwork Atlas has already downloaded and verified, as public <server>/media/<hash> links Health validates the URL and token

docs.title: Limits to know
docs.text:
• The app downloads artwork itself and refuses private addresses, so artwork needs a publicly reachable Atlas. Metadata works on a LAN.
  • Achievements are not part of the app's provider contract yet. Atlas serves the achievement list (GET /games/{id}/achievements); there is no per-user progress anywhere in Atlas.
  • Custom fields are available in the API (custom) but the app's metadata model has no slot for them.
  • The plugin sends no personal data: only titles, years and provider ids.

docs.title: Signing in to the Tracking App with Atlas
docs.text:
This needs no plugin. The app has first-class OpenID Connect support (Settings → Administration → Single sign-on), and Atlas is a standard provider. A plugin can't add login methods (plugins have no login hook), and none is needed.

It has been verified with the app's own client stack: the same Authlib registration the app uses (src/core/oidc.py) completes a login against a live Atlas, receiving the ID token and claims (tools/compat/tracking_app_oidc.py).

docs.title: Step by step
docs.text:
On Atlas

  1. Turn on Act as a sign-in provider (OIDC) in Admin → Settings → Federation. ATLAS_PUBLIC_URL must be the public https:// address.
  2. Admin → Sign-in sharing → Register application:
  3. Name: Unnamed Tracking App
  4. Redirect addresses: the exact callback the app shows, https://<your-app>/api/auth/oidc/callback/<slug> (choose the slug in step 3; e.g. atlas).
  5. Token signature: RS256
  6. Require PKCE: un-tick. The app's client authenticates with its secret and does not send PKCE.
  7. Copy the client id and secret.

In the Tracking App (Settings → Administration → Single sign-on → Add provider)

Field Value Provider name / slug Atlas / atlas Issuer / discovery URL https://atlas.example.org Client ID / secret from Atlas Scopes openid profile email Groups claim / admin group leave empty (Atlas sends no groups) User matching Username if the same people use the same names, otherwise Email Allow new users your choice Require verified email On if you only want addresses people have confirmed (Atlas sets email_verified accordingly) Login button text such as “Continue with Atlas”

docs.title: Things to expect
docs.text:
• The app requires an email claim: an Atlas user without an email address cannot sign in. Authority nodes require one anyway.
  • Users see Atlas's consent screen once per sign-in, then land in the app.
  • There is no group or admin mapping. Make administrators in the app.
  • Signing out of the app does not sign out of Atlas, and vice versa.

If something fails, see Sign-in sharing → Troubleshooting.

docs.title: Want this to be one click?
docs.text: A preset “Add Atlas” template in the app's SSO settings (pre-filling scopes and matching) would be a small change in the app itself, not in a plugin. It is not done; it would be a pull request to the app repository.

docs.title: The server won't start
docs.text: Message Fix ATLAS_PUBLIC_URL must be https in production Use the real https:// address, or ATLAS_ENVIRONMENT=dev while testing. an authority in production needs PostgreSQL Set ATLAS_DATABASE_URL=postgresql+psycopg://… (see compose.authority.yaml). production with open registration needs ATLAS_INITIAL_ADMIN Set the username that should administer the node (or close registration). ATLAS_TRUSTED_KEYS must list the upstream's key Pin the upstream with Admin → Peers instead, or set the key (from atlas node upstream).

docs.title: People can't sign up or contribute
docs.text:
• “an email address is required”: this node requires verified email; give one.
  • “confirm your email address before contributing”: open the link in the confirmation email (Profile shows a send again button). With outbox delivery nothing is sent; an administrator reads Admin → Email or marks the address confirmed.
  • “too many …”: a throttle; wait the number of seconds shown.
  • Their changes don't appear: they are waiting for review (new accounts) or were rejected (see My account → My proposals).

docs.title: Replication problems
docs.text: Admin → Peers shows each peer's last error. Common ones: not trusted (the node id changed or was never pinned), feed gap or rewind (the upstream was restored from an older backup; re-pin after confirming with its administrator), bad signature, token missing the sync scope, unreachable upstream (the node keeps serving and retries).

docs.title: Artwork doesn't show
docs.text: Images appear only after Atlas has downloaded and checked them (a background pass about once a minute, or atlas cache-media). Failures back off automatically. The source must be a public address; sizes above ATLAS_MEDIA_MAX_BYTES, non-images and SVG are refused.

docs.title: The API says 401/403/429
docs.text: 401: missing or invalid token (or the owner is suspended). 403: the token lacks the scope (see API reference). 429: rate limit; obey Retry-After.

docs.title: FAQ
docs.text:
Does Atlas store my playtime or library? No. Personal facts in submissions are discarded.

Can it track achievement completion? No: only the list and global percentages.

Can I use another database? SQLite and PostgreSQL only.

Can I run it without Docker? Yes: pip install . then atlas migrate and atlas serve (Python 3.12+).

How do I move from the old demo? atlas import-legacy path/to/demo-1.db.

Where are the screenshots from? The demo data in docs/guide/img, produced by the project's own browser tour.

docs.title: Browsing
docs.text:
Anyone can search and read: games, artwork, achievements, discussions and public profiles. Each game page shows the merged facts, identifiers (with links where they exist), achievements, a Where this came from table, and recent changes.

A phone-sized screen works the same way; the site follows your system's light or dark setting.

docs.title: Creating an account
docs.text:
Create account needs a username (3–32 letters, digits, -, _) and a password of at least the node's minimum length (10 by default). An email address is optional on a private node; central (authority) nodes require one and ask you to confirm it before you can contribute. We send a link; opening it shows a button to confirm (so mail scanners cannot confirm for you).

Forgot your password? on the sign-in page emails a link that works for one hour and once. It signs you out everywhere. The same message is shown whether or not the account exists.

docs.title: Suggesting changes
docs.text:
On a game page choose Suggest an edit. You can change core fields and any custom fields the administrators defined, and add a source or note for reviewers (link the store page or announcement: it speeds review). Add game proposes a new record; Suggest artwork and Add achievements are on the game page.

What happens next depends on your reputation:

You are Your change… new waits in the review queue (a limited number per day) trusted (reputation ≥ the node's threshold, 50 by default) applies at once, and can still be reverted; self-applied changes earn no reputation a reviewer applies at once

Reviewers see exactly what changes (old and new). You can withdraw a pending proposal and discuss it with reviewers on its page (only you and reviewers can see that thread).

docs.title: Reputation
docs.text:
• A reviewer approves your proposal: +5 (edit), +10 (new game), +3 (artwork), +5 (achievements).
  • Rejected: −2. Reverted later: −10 and the points it earned.
  • A moderator hides one of your comments: −3.

Reputation unlocks: immediate application (default 50) and review rights (default 500; admins can also promote people). Administrators can change every number.

docs.title: Lists, follows and your inbox
docs.text:
• Lists: Favourites and Wishlist exist for everyone; make more. Lists are private unless you make them public. They hold games only (completion lives in your tracker).
  • Follow a game or a person; changes show up in your Inbox (repeats within an hour fold into one entry). In Profile settings you can opt in to emails for them (confirmed addresses only).
  • Comments are plain text, up to 2000 characters, on games and (privately) on proposals. @name notifies someone. You can edit for 15 minutes, delete your own, and report others'. Three independent reports hide a comment until a moderator decides.

docs.title: Your profile and your data
docs.text: /u/<you> shows your reputation, badges and accepted contributions. In Profile settings you can hide it, write a short bio, download everything we hold about you (JSON) and delete your account. Deleting removes your profile, lists, follows, notifications and tokens and signs you out everywhere; your accepted contributions are public domain (CC0) and stay, detached from your name.

docs.title: Personal API tokens
docs.text: My account → API tokens creates read-only tokens for your own scripts. They cannot write (contribute through the site so changes are reviewed) and stop working if your account is suspended.

docs.title: Signing in with another node
docs.text: If your node's administrator enabled sign-in sharing, the sign-in page shows buttons such as Sign in with Central. See Sign-in sharing.

docs.title: Choose your setup
docs.text:
Atlas runs in two common shapes. Both use the same official container image; only the configuration differs.

Authoritative server Local node Who it's for a community or organisation running the shared, public source of truth one person, household or team; a private cache; optionally following a central node Role authority local People many accounts; open or closed registration usually just you Database PostgreSQL 16 SQLite in a volume Network public, HTTPS, domain name localhost or your LAN Email real SMTP (confirmed addresses are required to contribute) not needed Backups daily database dumps + restore drill copy the volume Publishes a change feed yes no Follows other nodes no yes (optional) Guide Authoritative server Local node

Not sure? Start with a local node; it takes five minutes and can follow a central node later. To see both working together before you commit to anything, try federation on one machine.

docs.title: What you get from the official image
docs.text:
• ghcr.io/obsoletelabs/unnamed_tracking_metadata for linux/amd64 and linux/arm64 (servers, laptops, Raspberry Pi, Apple silicon).
  • Runs as a non-root user, exposes port 8000, has a health check.
  • Contains the web site, API, migrations and the atlas command-line tool.
  • Built and smoke-tested by CI on every release, then scanned for known vulnerabilities.

See Ways to install (image, build from source, Python package), Official images for tags and pinning, and Proxmox LXC.

docs.title: The three files you need
docs.text:
For each setup there is a ready-made folder in the repository under deploy/:

Folder Contents deploy/authority/ compose.yaml (Atlas, PostgreSQL, Caddy with automatic HTTPS, daily backups), Caddyfile, .env.example, restore.sh deploy/local/ compose.yaml, .env.example deploy/lab/ compose.yaml: an authority and a local node on one machine each folder compose.build.yaml: add -f compose.build.yaml --build to build the image from source instead of pulling it

Each guide starts with git clone; the folder is all you use afterwards.

docs.title: After it's running
docs.text:
• Configure it from the browser: Administering.
  • Connect your apps: Tracking App.
  • Keep it healthy: Operations.

docs.title: Authoritative server
docs.text:
An authority is the public source of truth for a community: it accepts contributions and curation, publishes the signed change feed that mirrors and local nodes follow, and can sign people in to other software. This guide takes you from an empty server to a hardened, backed-up, federated deployment using the official images.

What you need

  • A Linux server (1 vCPU / 2 GB RAM is a reasonable starting point; no load testing has been done, so size for your own traffic) with Docker + Compose and ports 80 and 443 open.
  • A DNS name pointing at it (for example atlas.example.org).
  • An SMTP account for email (verification and password reset). Authorities require confirmed addresses before people can contribute.
  • About 30 minutes.

docs.title: 1. Get the deployment files
docs.text:
git clone -b v2 https://github.com/obsoletelabs/unnamed_tracking_metadata.git /opt/atlas-src
cd /opt/atlas-src/deploy/authority
cp .env.example .env

Work from this folder (/opt/atlas-src/deploy/authority) for the rest of the guide; copy it elsewhere if you prefer.

docs.title: 2. Fill in .env
docs.text:
Generate the secrets:

openssl rand -hex 24                                    # ATLAS_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_TOKEN
openssl rand -hex 24                                    # POSTGRES_PASSWORD
docker run --rm ghcr.io/obsoletelabs/unnamed_tracking_metadata:v2 atlas secret-key   # ATLAS_SECRET_KEY

Set at least:

ATLAS_DOMAIN=atlas.example.org
ATLAS_PUBLIC_URL=https://atlas.example.org
ATLAS_INITIAL_ADMIN=alice
ATLAS_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_TOKEN=…
ATLAS_SECRET_KEY=…
POSTGRES_PASSWORD=…
ATLAS_MAIL_BACKEND=smtp
ATLAS_SMTP_HOST=… ATLAS_SMTP_USER=… ATLAS_SMTP_PASSWORD=… ATLAS_MAIL_FROM=Atlas <noreply@example.org>
ATLAS_TAG=2.0.0        # pin a release

Keep .env safe and backed up

ATLAS_SECRET_KEY encrypts stored peer tokens and OIDC secrets; without it they cannot be read again. chmod 600 .env.

Production mode refuses to start unless the public URL is https://, the database is PostgreSQL, and (with open registration) an initial admin or bootstrap token is set. That is deliberate.

docs.title: 3. Start it
docs.text:
docker compose up -d
docker compose ps          # db healthy, migrate exited 0, atlas + caddy running
docker compose logs -f atlas

What runs: PostgreSQL, a one-shot migrate job (atlas migrate), Atlas (not published on the host; only the proxy can reach it, which is what makes trusting its forwarded headers safe), Caddy (automatic Let's Encrypt certificates for your domain), and a backup container (daily pg_dump, 14 days kept, in ./backups).

Check: https://atlas.example.org/api/v2/health returns {"status":"ok"…}, and https://atlas.example.org/api/v2/ready too.

Build from source instead

From a clone of the repository, in deploy/authority: docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.build.yaml up -d --build. The rest of this guide is identical.

docs.title: 4. First sign-in and basic setup
docs.text:
1. Open the site and Create account with the username in ATLAS_INITIAL_ADMIN and an email address. You are the administrator.
  2. Confirm your email (Admin → Email shows messages if SMTP isn't working yet; fix SMTP, then use Mark confirmed in the user list only as a stopgap).
  3. Admin → Settings: name, colours, logo, registration (open/closed), thresholds. Start with registration closed if you want to invite people first.
  4. Admin → Pages: edit About and Contribution rules.
  5. Admin → Fields: add media types or custom fields if you want them.
  6. Optionally add provider keys to .env (ATLAS_RAWG_API_KEY, ATLAS_IGDB_*, ATLAS_STEAM_API_KEY) and docker compose up -d.

docs.title: 5. Make it useful to others
docs.text: Goal How Let local nodes and mirrors follow you Admin → Tokens: create a token with scopes read + sync per follower; give them the address and your node id (Admin → Peers → This node) over a trusted channel. See Federation. Let apps read metadata A token with only read. The Tracking App plugin uses this. Let people sign in to other software with their account Settings → Act as a sign-in provider, then Admin → Sign-in sharing. See Sign-in sharing. Curators Promote trusted people (user list) or let reputation grant review rights.

docs.title: 6. Backups, and a restore drill
docs.text:
The backup container writes ./backups/atlas-YYYYmmdd-HHMMSS.dump daily. Copy them off the server (rsync, object storage) and back up the media volume too:

docker run --rm -v atlas_media:/m -v "$PWD":/out busybox tar czf /out/media.tgz -C /m .

Practise a restore on a scratch machine (same .env, same files):

./restore.sh backups/atlas-20261018-030000.dump     # replaces the database contents and restarts

The node's identity (the key followers pin) lives in the database, so restoring the database restores the identity.

docs.title: 7. Upgrading
docs.text:
# 1. back up (above)  2. read the release notes  3. change the tag
sed -i 's/^ATLAS_TAG=.*/ATLAS_TAG=2.1.0/' .env
docker compose pull && docker compose up -d     # migrate runs first, then Atlas restarts
docker compose logs --tail=50 migrate atlas

Migrations only move forward. If something is wrong, restore the backup and put the old tag back.

docs.title: 8. Hardening checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] .env is mode 600 and not in a repository.
  • [ ] Only ports 80/443 (and SSH) are reachable from outside; PostgreSQL is not published.
  • [ ] SMTP works (send yourself a password reset) and SPF/DKIM are set for your sending domain.
  • [ ] Off-site backups and a tested restore.
  • [ ] ATLAS_TAG pinned; you know how you'll learn about security updates.
  • [ ] Registration policy decided (open/closed) and the Rules page written.
  • [ ] At least two administrators (so one can recover the other's account).
  • [ ] An uptime check on /api/v2/ready.

docs.title: Scaling out
docs.text: More replicas of the atlas service work behind the same proxy: sessions, tokens and rate limits live in the database. Keep ATLAS_AUTO_MIGRATE=false (the compose file does) so only the migrate job changes the schema. Writes are serialised by a database lock, which is fine for metadata and the first limit you would meet under very heavy ingestion. See Operations.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Likely cause Caddy can't get a certificate DNS doesn't point here yet, or 80/443 are blocked. atlas keeps restarting docker compose logs atlas: usually one of the production checks (HTTPS URL, PostgreSQL, initial admin). People never get email SMTP settings (Admin → Email shows the error per message). Followers report not trusted / gap They pinned a different node id, or you restored an older backup. See Federation.

docs.title: Where they are
docs.text:
ghcr.io/obsoletelabs/unnamed_tracking_metadata

Built by the repository's Publish container workflow (multi-architecture linux/amd64 + linux/arm64, with build provenance and an SBOM attached by BuildKit), smoke-tested by starting the published image and calling its health endpoint, and scanned with Trivy (High/Critical, fixed vulnerabilities fail the build).

docs.title: Tags
docs.text:
Tag Meaning Use it for 2.0.0, 2.0 a release (git tag v2.0.0); 2.0 follows patch releases production: pin an exact version latest the newest build of the main branch trying things out v2 the newest build of the v2 branch (the current development line, until it is merged to main) following development sha-<short> one exact commit reproducing a build

Pin in production

Put ATLAS_TAG=2.0.0 (or whichever release you tested) in .env. Upgrade deliberately, after a backup, by changing the number. Never run an authority on a moving tag.

You can also pin by digest (ghcr.io/…@sha256:…), which cannot change underneath you.

docs.title: Pulling
docs.text:
If the repository/package is public, docker pull ghcr.io/obsoletelabs/unnamed_tracking_metadata:2.0.0 just works.

While it is private, sign in first with a GitHub personal access token that has the read:packages scope:

echo "$GITHUB_PAT" | docker login ghcr.io -u <your-github-username> --password-stdin

(The deploy folders use whichever image your login allows.)

docs.title: Using your own build instead
docs.text: Every deploy/ folder has a compose.build.yaml: docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.build.yaml up -d --build. Details and the plain docker build route: Ways to install. There is also a Python package.

docs.title: What's inside
docs.text:
• Python 3.12 slim base, a pre-built virtual environment (no compilers in the final image), no shell history or build tools.
  • User atlas (uid 10001); working directory and default SQLite database in /data (a volume).
  • CMD ["atlas", "serve", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "8000"]; the atlas CLI can run one-off jobs: docker compose exec atlas atlas <command> (commands).
  • HEALTHCHECK calls /api/v2/health.

docs.title: The documentation image
docs.text:
Each build of the documentation site is also published, so you can read these docs offline or host them yourself:

docker run --rm -p 8080:8080 ghcr.io/obsoletelabs/unnamed_tracking_metadata-docs:v2   # http://localhost:8080

docs.title: Ways to install Atlas
docs.text:
Pick one. The official Docker image is the preferred route; the others exist for people who want to build it themselves or do not use Docker.

When to choose it Tested here 1. Official Docker image (recommended) almost always; the same artifact CI built, smoke-tested and scanned yes: published by CI, started and checked in CI 2. Docker image built from source you want to audit or modify the code, or can't reach the registry yes 3. Python package (wheel) no Docker (a VM, a bare LXC, a Raspberry Pi), or you prefer systemd yes: clean-environment install, migrations, web UI 4. Proxmox LXC you run Proxmox method B/C below on any recent Proxmox; the OCI method needs Proxmox VE 9.1+ — see Proxmox LXC

Every example in this guide (the deploy/ folders) works with routes 1 and 2 by changing one command.

docs.title: 1. Official Docker image (recommended)
docs.text:
git clone -b v2 https://github.com/obsoletelabs/unnamed_tracking_metadata.git
cd unnamed_tracking_metadata/deploy/local        # or authority/ or lab/
cp .env.example .env                             # edit it
docker compose up -d

The compose files pull ghcr.io/obsoletelabs/unnamed_tracking_metadata:${ATLAS_TAG}. Pin ATLAS_TAG to a release. If the package is private you must docker login ghcr.io first (Official images).

docs.title: 2. Build the image from source
docs.text:
Same folders, one extra file:

cd unnamed_tracking_metadata/deploy/local
cp .env.example .env
docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.build.yaml up -d --build

compose.build.yaml points the service at the repository's Dockerfile (two stages, non-root, health check) and tags it atlas:local. Behind a restrictive network, build once by hand: docker build --network=host -t atlas:local . and then start with the same two -f flags (without --build). To update: git pull then rerun the command.

Or build and run the image yourself:

docker build -t atlas:local .
docker run -d --name atlas -p 127.0.0.1:8000:8000 -v atlas-data:/data \
  -e ATLAS_ROLE=local -e ATLAS_INITIAL_ADMIN=alice atlas:local

docs.title: 3. Python package (no Docker)
docs.text:
Needs Python 3.12 or newer (Debian 13 or Ubuntu 24.04 have it; Debian 12 does not).

Install the wheel from a release or CI artifact, or directly from the repository:

python3 -m venv /opt/atlas/venv
/opt/atlas/venv/bin/pip install atlas_metadata-2.0.0-py3-none-any.whl
# or, from git (a private repository needs a token in the URL):
/opt/atlas/venv/bin/pip install "atlas-metadata @ git+https://github.com/obsoletelabs/unnamed_tracking_metadata@v2"

Releases publish the wheel and source archive on the GitHub release page; every build also uploads them as the python-package artifact of the Python package workflow. The wheel contains the web site, migrations and CLI (atlas); CI installs it into a clean environment and starts it on every build.

Configure with environment variables (a file is easiest) and run:

mkdir -p /etc/atlas /var/lib/atlas
cat > /etc/atlas/atlas.env <<'ENV'
ATLAS_ROLE=local
ATLAS_PUBLIC_URL=http://localhost:8000
ATLAS_DATABASE_URL=sqlite:////var/lib/atlas/atlas.db
ATLAS_MEDIA_DIR=/var/lib/atlas/media
ATLAS_INITIAL_ADMIN=alice
ATLAS_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_TOKEN=change-me-to-32+-random-characters
ENV
chmod 600 /etc/atlas/atlas.env
set -a; . /etc/atlas/atlas.env; set +a
/opt/atlas/venv/bin/atlas migrate
/opt/atlas/venv/bin/atlas serve --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8000

docs.title: Keep it running with systemd
docs.text:
# /etc/systemd/system/atlas.service
[Unit]
Description=Atlas metadata server
After=network-online.target
Wants=network-online.target

[Service]
User=atlas
Group=atlas
EnvironmentFile=/etc/atlas/atlas.env
WorkingDirectory=/var/lib/atlas
ExecStartPre=/opt/atlas/venv/bin/atlas migrate
ExecStart=/opt/atlas/venv/bin/atlas serve --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000
Restart=on-failure
RestartSec=3
NoNewPrivileges=true
ProtectSystem=strict
ProtectHome=true
PrivateTmp=true
ReadWritePaths=/var/lib/atlas

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

useradd --system --home /var/lib/atlas --shell /usr/sbin/nologin atlas
chown -R atlas:atlas /var/lib/atlas
systemctl daemon-reload && systemctl enable --now atlas
journalctl -u atlas -f

Upgrade: pip install --upgrade <new wheel> then systemctl restart atlas (migrations run first). Back up /var/lib/atlas and /etc/atlas.

An authority from the Python package?

Possible (PostgreSQL, a reverse proxy, ATLAS_ENVIRONMENT=production), but the supported, tested production path is the container deployment in Authoritative server.

docs.title: Try federation on one machine
docs.text:
The lab runs an authority and a local node side by side on your computer so you can watch replication, overrides, shared fields and sign-in sharing work, before deploying anything. Everything here was exercised end to end against the official image.

Lab only

Plain HTTP, development mode, well-known tokens. Both ports bind to 127.0.0.1. Do not expose it.

docs.title: Start it
docs.text:
git clone -b v2 https://github.com/obsoletelabs/unnamed_tracking_metadata.git
cd unnamed_tracking_metadata/deploy/lab
docker compose up -d
Address Administrator Authority http://authority.lab.localhost:8001 register alice Local node http://localhost:8002 register bob

(*.localhost names resolve to your own machine in browsers and curl. The local node reaches the authority under the same name through a fixed lab address, so one address works for both the browser and the server.)

Lab tokens: authority lab-bootstrap-token-0123456789abcdef0123456789, local lab-local-token-0123456789abcdef0123456789abcd.

No registry access?

Build the image instead: docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.build.yaml up -d --build from deploy/lab in a clone of the repository.

docs.title: 1. Put curated data on the authority
docs.text:
Register alice at the authority. Then add records through the API as a curator:

AUTH=http://authority.lab.localhost:8001; T=lab-bootstrap-token-0123456789abcdef0123456789
curl -s $AUTH/api/v2/observations -H "Authorization: Bearer $T" -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{
  "connection": {"source_kind":"metadata","source":"curator","source_scope":"lab"},
  "observations": [{"external_id":"1","title":"Hades","release_date":"2020-09-17","facts":{"developer":"Supergiant"}}]}'

Also add one non-curated record (source playnite, kind plugin) to see that it does not replicate.

docs.title: 2. Let the local node follow it
docs.text:
1. On the authority create a token: Admin → Tokens, scopes read + sync (or POST /api/v2/tokens).
  2. On the local node (register bob): Admin → Peers → Add a peer, address http://authority.lab.localhost:8001, paste the token → Look up node.
  3. Compare the node id shown with the authority's (Admin → Peers → This node there). Choose Trust this node and replicate from it.
  4. Wait a few seconds (the lab syncs every 5 s) or press Sync now.

Check: http://localhost:8002 now lists Hades with the same id as the authority; the non-curated record is absent.

docs.title: 3. Watch changes flow
docs.text:
• On the authority, pin a value (a game page → Curation → Pinned fields) or edit as the administrator: the local node updates within seconds.
  • On the authority, Admin → Fields: add a custom field Engine. It appears on the local node (/api/v2/schema, edit forms).

docs.title: 4. Overrides stay local
docs.text: On the local node pin a different title on the same game. The local page shows yours; the authority is unchanged, and a later upstream change does not overwrite your override.

docs.title: 5. Sign in to the local node with an authority account
docs.text:
1. Authority: Settings already has the provider on. Register dave (with an email) as an ordinary user.
  2. Local node: Admin → Sign-in sharing → Look up provider, address http://authority.lab.localhost:8001. It shows the redirect address to register.
  3. Authority: Admin → Sign-in sharing → Register application: that redirect address, signature EdDSA. Copy the client id and secret.
  4. Local node: enter the client id and secret in the confirmation form, tick Create an account on first sign-in, Add provider.
  5. In a private window open the local node, choose the provider button, sign in as dave on the authority, Allow. You land on the local node signed in as dave.

docs.title: Reset or remove
docs.text:
docker compose down        # stop, keep data
docker compose down -v     # stop and delete everything

docs.title: Local node
docs.text: A local node is your own Atlas: private, cheap to run, and able to cache provider data. It can run entirely on its own, or follow a central authority so you receive its curated records and still keep your own overrides. It runs fine on a Raspberry Pi (the image is built for arm64).

docs.title: 1. Get the files
docs.text:
git clone -b v2 https://github.com/obsoletelabs/unnamed_tracking_metadata.git
cd unnamed_tracking_metadata/deploy/local
cp .env.example .env

docs.title: 2. Configure
docs.text:
Edit .env:

ATLAS_PUBLIC_URL=http://localhost:8000
ATLAS_INITIAL_ADMIN=alice
ATLAS_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_TOKEN=<openssl rand -hex 24>
ATLAS_TAG=2.0.0        # or v2 while following development

Optional: ATLAS_SECRET_KEY (run docker run --rm ghcr.io/obsoletelabs/unnamed_tracking_metadata:v2 atlas secret-key) if you will store peer tokens or sign-in secrets in the admin UI; provider keys (ATLAS_RAWG_API_KEY, ATLAS_STEAM_API_KEY, ATLAS_IGDB_*).

docs.title: 3. Start
docs.text:
docker compose up -d

Open http://localhost:8000, Create account as alice (administrator). Email isn't required on a local node, and nothing is sent: messages appear under Admin → Email.

By default the port is bound to 127.0.0.1 (this machine only). To share on your network set ATLAS_BIND=0.0.0.0 (or your LAN address) in .env and put a firewall rule or reverse proxy in front if others you don't trust share that network.

Build from source instead

docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.build.yaml up -d --build builds the image from a checkout of the repository rather than pulling it. No Docker at all? See Ways to install and Proxmox LXC.

docs.title: 4. Use it
docs.text:
• Add data: Add game on the site, or ask a provider through the API (POST /api/v2/providers/steam/fetch). Provider data is cached on your node only.
  • Connect the Tracking App: create a read token (Admin → Tokens) and use the plugin.
  • Make it yours: Administering: colours, pages, fields.

docs.title: 5. Follow a central node (optional)
docs.text:
You need from the authority's administrator: its address, its node id, and a token with scopes read + sync.

  1. Set ATLAS_SECRET_KEY in .env and docker compose up -d (so the token can be stored encrypted).
  2. Admin → Peers → Add a peer: address + token → Look up node.
  3. Compare the node id shown with the one you were given, then Trust this node and replicate from it.
  4. Sync now. From then on it follows automatically (every 60 s).

What you get: the authority's curated records, merges, pins, artwork, achievements, custom fields and media types, with the same ids. What you keep: provider data, private overrides and your accounts. The authority never receives anything from you. Details: Federation.

docs.title: 6. Sign in with a central account (optional)
docs.text: If the authority is a sign-in provider you can let your users sign in with their account there: Sign-in sharing.

docs.title: Backups and upgrades
docs.text:
Everything lives in the atlas-data volume (database and cached images).

docker compose stop atlas
docker run --rm -v atlas-local_atlas-data:/d -v "$PWD":/out busybox tar czf /out/atlas-data.tgz -C /d .
docker compose start atlas

Upgrade: change ATLAS_TAG, then docker compose pull && docker compose up -d (migrations run automatically on a SQLite node).

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Fix Port already in use set ATLAS_PORT=8080 in .env. docker compose pull says denied sign in to the registry (Official images) or build your own image. Peer says not trusted / bad signature wrong node id pinned, or the authority's identity changed (it was restored from nothing). Confirm with its administrator and re-add the peer. Artwork missing artwork is downloaded in the background after the record exists; it needs outbound internet.

docs.title: Running Atlas in a Proxmox LXC
docs.text:
Three ways, from the newest to the most conventional. All give you a small, self-contained Atlas on your Proxmox host, ideal for a local node.

Method Needs Notes A. OCI image as an LXC Proxmox VE 9.1 or newer the new "application container" feature; runs the official image directly, no Docker inside B. Debian/Ubuntu LXC + Python package any Proxmox VE with a Debian 13 / Ubuntu 24.04 template the most conventional; systemd service C. LXC with Docker + the compose files any Proxmox VE familiar, a little heavier

What has and has not been tested

The Atlas side of each method has been tested (the image runs and passes its health check; the Python package installs into a clean environment and serves the site). I could not run Proxmox itself while writing this, so the Proxmox steps below follow Proxmox's documented behaviour and are marked where I am less certain. Proxmox's OCI feature is labelled a technology preview and changes between releases: if a menu or option differs from what is written here, trust your Proxmox version's documentation and tell us so we can fix this page.

docs.title: Common preparation
docs.text:
• Resources: 1 core, 1 GB RAM, 4 GB disk is plenty for a personal node (the cache grows with artwork).
  • Network: a bridge (vmbr0) with DHCP or a fixed address. You will reach Atlas at http://<container-ip>:8000.
  • Data lives in /data (database and cached images). Keep it on a mount point so you can upgrade or rebuild the container without losing it, and so you can back it up.
  • Decide a public URL (http://<container-ip>:8000, or the name you put in front of it with a proxy) and put it in ATLAS_PUBLIC_URL.

docs.title: A. OCI image as an LXC (Proxmox VE 9.1+)
docs.text: Proxmox VE 9.1 can create an LXC container straight from an OCI/Docker image. It runs the image's own entry point as the container's main process (an application container): no init system, no Docker.

docs.title: 1. Pull the image
docs.text:
In the web UI: Datacenter → your storage (one that allows Container templates, usually local) → CT Templates → Pull from OCI Registry.

  • Reference: ghcr.io/obsoletelabs/unnamed_tracking_metadata:2.0.0 (pin a release; v2 follows development)
  • File name: atlas-2.0.0 (anything you like)

Private registry

While the package is private, anonymous pulls fail. Either make the package public, or create the template another way (for example skopeo copy docker://ghcr.io/…:2.0.0 oci-archive:/var/lib/vz/template/cache/atlas-2.0.0.tar after skopeo login ghcr.io), whichever your Proxmox version accepts as a container template. Confirm against your version's documentation.

docs.title: 2. Create the container
docs.text:
Create CT → on the Template step choose the image you pulled. Then:

Setting Value Unprivileged container yes (recommended) CPU / memory 1 core, 1024 MB Root disk 4 GB Network your bridge; DHCP or a static address Mount point add mp0: a volume of 4–10 GB (or a bind mount of a host directory), path /data Start after creation no (set the environment first)

docs.title: 3. Environment variables
docs.text:
In the container's Options → Environment (application containers expose the image's environment and entry point there), add:

ATLAS_ROLE=local
ATLAS_PUBLIC_URL=http://192.168.1.50:8000
ATLAS_DATABASE_URL=sqlite:////data/atlas.db
ATLAS_MEDIA_DIR=/data/media
ATLAS_INITIAL_ADMIN=alice
ATLAS_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_TOKEN=<openssl rand -hex 24>

Leave the entry point/command at the image default (atlas serve --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000).

docs.title: 4. Fix data permissions, then start
docs.text:
The image runs as the unprivileged user atlas (uid 10001). In an unprivileged container Proxmox maps container uid N to host uid 100000 + N, so on a bind-mounted host directory give that user ownership:

mkdir -p /srv/atlas-data && chown -R 110001:110001 /srv/atlas-data
pct set <ctid> -mp0 /srv/atlas-data,mp=/data

(For a storage-backed volume Proxmox sets ownership for you; if Atlas cannot write /data, this is the first thing to check. If your Proxmox runs the entry point as root, no change is needed.)

Start the container and open http://<container-ip>:8000. Register alice: she is the administrator.

docs.title: 5. Upgrading (Method A)
docs.text: Application containers are not updated in place. To move to a new release: pull the new image tag as a template, create a new container from it with the same settings and the same /data mount point (detach it from the old container and attach it to the new one, or bind-mount the same host directory), start it, and remove the old container once you are happy. Take a backup first.

docs.title: 6. Backups (Method A)
docs.text:
• A storage-backed mount point with Backup ticked is included in Proxmox backups (vzdump) with the container.
  • A bind mount is not part of vzdump: back it up yourself (tar czf atlas-data.tgz -C /srv/atlas-data . while the container is stopped).

docs.title: B. Debian/Ubuntu LXC with the Python package
docs.text:
Works on any Proxmox VE. Atlas needs Python 3.12+, so use the Debian 13 or Ubuntu 24.04 template (Debian 12 ships Python 3.11).

  1. Create CT from a Debian 13 / Ubuntu 24.04 template: unprivileged, 1 core, 1 GB, 4 GB disk, your network. Start it and open its console (or SSH).
  2. Install prerequisites: 
    apt update && apt install -y python3 python3-venv python3-pip curl ca-certificates
  3. Install Atlas and the service exactly as in Ways to install → Python package: the virtual environment in /opt/atlas, the environment file in /etc/atlas, data in /var/lib/atlas, and the atlas.service unit.
  4. systemctl enable --now atlas, then browse to http://<container-ip>:8000.

Data and backups: /var/lib/atlas is on the container's root disk, so a normal Proxmox container backup covers it. Upgrading: pip install --upgrade <wheel> and systemctl restart atlas; snapshot the container first.

docs.title: C. LXC with Docker and the compose files
docs.text:
1. Create a Debian 13 / Ubuntu 24.04 container, unprivileged, and enable Options → Features → Nesting and keyctl (required for Docker inside LXC).
  2. Install Docker (curl -fsSL https://get.docker.com | sh) and clone the repository.
  3. Use the deploy/local folder: Local node (official image) or add -f compose.build.yaml --build to build from source.

Docker inside LXC works well but adds a layer; prefer A or B unless you already standardise on compose.

docs.title: Reaching it from elsewhere
docs.text: The container has its own address. For other machines, either browse to http://<container-ip>:8000 directly (a trusted LAN), or put a reverse proxy in front (the Proxmox host, another container running Caddy or nginx with HTTPS). Set ATLAS_PUBLIC_URL to the address people actually use. Do not expose port 8000 to the internet without HTTPS.

docs.title: Connecting the rest
docs.text:
• Follow a central node: Local node → Follow a central node.
  • The Tracking App plugin: Tracking App.
  • Check it's healthy: curl http://<container-ip>:8000/api/v2/ready.
